Six people, including two children, have been found dead after a plane crashed off the coast of Mississippi on Tuesday, the US Coast Guard says.

The Cessna 210 was on its way from New Orleans to Fort Myers, Florida, according to the flight tracking website FlightAware. Air traffic control lost touch with it at about 15:45 (21:45 GMT) and it later went down in the Gulf of Mexico between Pascagoula and Horn Island, officials said.

Divers found the bodies of four adults and two boys, aged 8 and 10, in the fuselage, said Coast Guard spokesperson Juan Ros.

Rescuers spent hours searching for the group and initially only found three life jackets, a life raft and the plane's cabin floating on the water, he said.

Cmdr Trevor Blount, the Coast Guard rescue mission co-ordinator, said: "While this is not the outcome any of us had hoped for, we are grateful for the strong interagency co-ordination that enabled us to swiftly locate those aboard the aircraft and provide closure to their families."

Australia and the Solomon Islands have signed a new treaty on security and economics

The Solomon Islands has signed a "historic" treaty with Australia, after reportedly telling China it was ending a controversial security pact signed in 2022.

At a press conference in Canberra on Wednesday, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Solomon Islands counterpart Matthew Wale said the new treaty would ensure that Australia was the Pacific nation's "security partner of choice".

In 2022 the Solomon Islands, then under the leadership of now-Opposition Leader Manasseh Sogavare, signed a security and policing pact with Beijing .

There were fears the pact gave China a crucial military and strategic foothold in the Pacific amid a battle for influence in the region with the US.

On Tuesday, Australian media outlets reported that Honiara had told Beijing it would not renew the pact, understood to be expiring in April 2027.

Wale told reporters on Wednesday there were "ongoing discussions" with China but he was "unable to talk about" the pact, because of a non-disclosure agreement.

He said the treaty with Australia provided a reset after several years in which the Solomon Islands had been a point of "uncertainty and doubt in the region".

Albanese said the treaty would strengthen the two countries' security partnership.

"Backing our Pacific neighbours is an investment in Australia's own security and our own prosperity."

"We'll do that in a way that completely respects Solomon Islands sovereignty and its right to make its own decisions."

On Tuesday China's foreign ministry spokesman, Guo Jiukan, did not confirm or deny that the pact had been terminated.

"There is no element of geopolitical rivalry or bloc confrontation in cooperation between China and Pacific island countries, including the Solomon Islands," Guo said.

The pact was never publicly released, but leaked excerpts revealed it gave China extensive involvement in security and policing including deploying its own officers to the Solomon Islands, and allowed it to establish a quasi military base.

It was a "massive coup" for Beijing, said Lowy Institute Research Fellow, Dr Connor Graham, but its unprecedented scale sparked alarm in the Pacific and the West.

Wednesday's treaty had delivered "an enormous win for Canberra", and "closes the loop" on a series of security deals Canberra signed with Pacific nations in the wake of the Solomons-China pact.

"That [China pact] was the thing that put fear in the hearts of diplomats in Washington and Canberra," he told the BBC.

William Yang, the International Crisis Group's Senior Analyst for North East Asia, said the end of China's "flagship" Pacific deal and the signing of the new treaty also reaffirmed the Pacific's "longstanding consensus-based decision-making model, especially in the security space".

Under the new treaty, the Solomon Islands commits to prior consultation with Australia on critical infrastructure and to ensure any security cooperations are with Pacific Islands Forum members. China is a dialogue partner but not a member of the forum.

Honiara also commits to its sensitive infrastructure remaining "free from militarisation, any form of foreign interference or unauthorised access", and to not permit its territory to be used for any foreign military or security base.

The Solomons will receive support for its free education system and sports programs, improved visa arrangements, and support for the expansion of affordable and renewable energy and infrastructure development.

Earlier this week the ABC reported the package promised more than A$980m (£460.7m, $648,000) in additional funding, citing leaked text messages. The BBC has not independently verified the text messages.

Wale visited Australia to sign the treaty, accompanied by two dozen Solomons MPs. He and Albanese said the size of the delegation demonstrated that the treaty had strong support from the country's parliament, after years of political instability - largely driven by disagreement over the country's relationship with China .

Watch: BBC reporter investigates deaths of family members in Russia-Ukraine war

I am sitting on my balcony in Kyiv looking at a photo of a garden in the village I grew up in, in eastern Ukraine. The plot is overgrown with thick grass, and two wooden stakes are planted in the ground. Despite the warm sunshine, I find myself shivering.

The woman who sent me the photo says the stakes mark the graves of my grandparents, killed as the Ukrainian-Russian front line reached our little community. Not far away, in another garden in the village, the body of my father, Serezha, is buried in a greenhouse.

The photo Anastasiya was sent of her grandparents' graves

I cover the Russia-Ukraine war for the BBC World Service, but found myself in the middle of that story in February last year when my mother sent me a devastating text message.

"Granny, grandad and Serezha are gone. Now there is no-one left," it said.

Because not only had I lost three beloved family members, my mother blamed Ukraine for their deaths - the country where I was born and have lived for most of my life.

Mum was born in Siberia. From the moment Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, she had supported Russia in the conflict.

Anastasiya (bottom left) with her father (top left) and grandparents (right) before the war

Backing Moscow is not that unusual in the Donbas region - the predominantly Russian-speaking part of eastern Ukraine where my village Dachne is located.

After pro-Russian forces captured large parts of the Donbas in 2014, many of those who stayed supported Moscow over Kyiv, a stance cemented by exposure to Russian state TV.

Now the Russians occupy almost 80% of Donetsk - the part of the Donbas where my village is. Over the past nearly five years, since Russia's full-scale invasion, entire towns and cities have been razed to the ground , external .

The remains of Anastasiya's family home are circled in a frame of a video, filmed by Ukraine's 33rd Mechanised Brigade on 27 January 2025

I had already fallen out with my sister Sasha, who had been living in Moscow with her young family when the war broke out. She refused to take sides - I felt hurt and cut her off.

But earlier this year, around the first anniversary of dad's death, Sasha unexpectedly texted me. We started talking over text about our childhood - the way things used to be. I realised I was not angry with her anymore. She too was grieving, missing dad just as much as I was.

Anastasiya's father Serezha - he stayed in Dachne to look after his elderly parents

I told her I wanted to make a documentary about dad and she was very supportive. I knew then that I had an ally on my journey. But we decided not to tell our mum just yet.

I started looking for witnesses to the events in Dachne that took place in January 2025, the month dad is believed to have been killed. It was not easy. It was a village of a few hundred people, but many had left, others had died, and those who remained had limited phone signals.

Russia publicly announced the capture of Dachne on 14 February and it has remained under Moscow's control ever since.

This meant it was impossible for me to travel there in person. So I began trying to contact my family's neighbours.

Anastasiya could not safely travel back to Dachne, so she worked through contacts in village group chats

In a Dachne village messaging chat, I found the number of a man I'll call Misha. I was told he had been with my father on the day he died. Speaking to the BBC could put him in danger with the Russian occupiers, so I did not tell him I worked for the BBC or that I was recording our call.

Misha told me that on 26 January he had looked in on my father and realised he had been injured. Serezha told him he had been "clipped" by a drone, and had asked Misha to bring a first aid kit, he said.

It is impossible to know which side was operating the drone that killed my father, but we do know that Russian drones were constantly targeting the village at that time.

"I asked if the wound was serious. He [Serezha] said it wasn't," said Misha - but then recalling how, when he had returned to check on my father a couple of hours later, he had found him dead.

With the help of two other villagers, Misha said they had buried him in the greenhouse.

"I'm sorry I couldn't save him," Misha told me.

BBC Eye Investigations: Who Killed My Family?

BBC journalist Anastasiya Gribanova investigates who killed her father and grandparents in Ukraine, uncovering painful accounts as she tries to reunite her divided family.

Watch on BBC iPlayer or listen on BBC Sounds now (UK only)

If you are outside of the UK, listen to the Who Killed My Family podcast here

Watch our YouTube documentary here , external

As for my grandparents, my investigations suggested the events surrounding their deaths may have been more complicated.

Their house, on the eastern side of Dachne, had been destroyed. Neighbours told me they had escaped to another home on the same street.

I eventually reached a woman I'll call Lina, who lived nearby and was the last person, as far as I know, who saw my grandparents alive.

She could not recall what this date was, but knew it was in the second half of January.

At this time, she said, "the Russians were fully advancing - the edges of the village were being shelled. Then the Ukrainian soldiers moved from the edge of the village into the centre. They hid in people's yards and used side streets to avoid drones."

She said two soldiers entered her property. They had not been wearing any identifying insignia but had been speaking Ukrainian, she said - a language that Lina described as "Bandera", a derogatory term for Ukrainians.

"You're going to have to leave. Why are you still here?" Lina said they had asked her.

She said one had pointed a machine gun at her as she had stood outside her house, while another had gone to see my grandparents. She told me she had feared for her life and then fled her house for the night.

The following day, she told me she had returned to my grandparents' street to check on them.

She had found the door to the house they had been staying in open, she said, despite the freezing conditions.

With drones buzzing overhead, Lina said she had not dared look inside, but had later heard from neighbours that my grandparents had been found dead. She believed it had been the Ukrainian soldiers who visited her house who had shot them.

Another neighbour, who I will call Maria, described discovering their bodies - my grandmother in bed, covered in a blanket, and my grandfather lying on the floor in a pool of now-dried blood.

Maria also believed Ukrainian soldiers had killed them - because, she said, that she too had felt threatened by Ukrainian troops at the time.

"If they had seen me they would have killed me too."

Her theory was that my grandparents had irritated the troops in some way.

"Your grandparents caught them in a bad mood because your grandfather was always asking to be evacuated. And [the soldiers] were, you know, high. They were taking drugs. So your grandparents got in their way," she told me.

Most of the other people in the village I spoke to also believe Ukrainian soldiers killed them, though their testimony is not based on direct evidence.

The new local mayor, appointed by the Russian occupiers when they finally took control of Dachne in February, said she had been present at my grandparents' burial the following month, and said half of my grandmother's skull was missing.

These accounts of how they might have died in January 2025 were deeply disturbing, though no-one had witnessed their deaths and the information I was given could not be independently verified.

The villagers I spoke to - now living in occupied territory - did say there had been some tensions between themselves and Ukrainian troops at the time, because the soldiers had viewed those who remained in Dachne as supporters of Russia.

The clinical causes of my grandparents' deaths are unclear.

Their bodies were not exhumed for nearly 20 months, when the local authorities sent them to a morgue in the occupied region, where a basic autopsy was carried out by a forensics expert.

He told me that my grandmother had died of an explosives injury to the skull - but could not specify its cause.

As for my grandfather, it said his body had shown no obvious signs of injury.

I compared two satellite images of the house in which their bodies were found - from just before and just after when they are believed to have died - and could detect no significant damage to the building in the second image.

I also spoke to a villager who said he had buried my grandparents.

He said he did not know anything about who killed them.

"I wasn't there. But why would you kill old people?" he asked.

Anastasiya does not know if she will ever be able to give her grandparents (pictured) a dignified burial

I examined military maps from DeepStateMap.Live, an open-source Ukrainian resource, and US think tank Institute for the Study of War. They suggested Ukrainian forces still held the street where my grandparents lived during the week they had died, although the front line had been shifting rapidly.

My colleagues helped me identify the Russian military units that went on to capture Dachne. We found telephone numbers of Russian soldiers. But none of them agreed to speak to me.

A soldier from the 33rd Mechanised Brigade, who gave his name simply as Vlad, said his unit had still been in Dachne at the time my grandparents were believed to have died and that the Russians had been swiftly advancing.

Another Ukrainian soldier I spoke to also confirmed Ukraine's troops had still been in control of some parts of Dachne in late January.

We put our findings on the deaths of my grandparents to the Ukrainian military.

It said it had no verified evidence on how they died, or which implicated its servicemen during the "intense hostilities". It added that investigating allegations of wrongdoing was the role of law enforcement.

We also approached Russia's ministry of defence and Russia's embassy in London for comment - they did not respond.

Sisters Sasha (right) and Anastasiya were reunited at Belgrade Airport

The Donetsk regional prosecutor's office, which is now based outside Russian-controlled territory, has documented alleged Russian war crimes reported by eyewitnesses in villages around Dachne during December 2024 and January 2025 - including the killing of five civilians in a basement in the nearby village of Kostyantynopilske.

However, Ukrainian investigators have no equivalent cases registered in Dachne during that period. They have documented only three deaths there. My father and grandparents are not among them.

Their bodies lie in occupied territory, and I do not know if I will ever be able to say goodbye properly and bury them with dignity.

There is little more I can do for them, except one thing - mend my relationship with my sister and my mother.

Almost three years after I last saw my sister, I fly to Belgrade where she now lives.

Anastasiya (left) and her sister Sasha look through photos of their father

She is waiting for me at the airport, holding lilies, and a plate with a silly nickname on it that she gave me when we were children. We hug, cry and laugh. It feels as if something between us is finally falling back into place

At her flat, we look through family photographs and talk about my investigation and what I was able to find. My grief is still there, but it hurts a little less. I'm no longer carrying it alone.

"Are you ready?" Sasha asks. She rings our mother - who has also moved to Serbia - and puts the phone on speaker.

"Hi, Mum. It's Nastya," I say. First there is silence. Then I hear her crying. "Nastya, my darling, hello," she replies.

Perezida wa Repubulika, Paul Kagame, yasabye urubyiruko rwa Afurika kudategereza ko hari abandi bazarugenera ejo hazaza, ahubwo ko rukwiye gufata iya mbere mu kwiyubakira ubuzima rwifuza no kugira uruhare mu guhindura Umugabane n’isi muri rusange.

Yabigarutseho mu nama ya YouthConnekt Africa 2026 yabereye i Kigali, kuri uyu wa Gatatu tariki 25 Ugushyingo 2026 agaragaza ko ibyo Afurika imaze kugeraho kugeza ubu byaturutse ku kuba Abanyafurika barafashe inshingano zo kwiyubakira ejo hazaza habo.

Perezida Kagame yavuze ko ubushakashatsi buherutse gukorwa mu bihugu bitandukanye bya Afurika bugaragaza ko urubyiruko rw’uyu munsi rurushijeho kugira icyizere cy’ejo hazaza kandi rukaba rwifuza kugira uruhare mu kugena ahazaza harwo.

Yavuze ko iyo myumvire ari yo ikwiye kuranga urubyiruko, kuko intsinzi nyakuri itangirira ku muntu wiyemeje kwiyubakira ubuzima yifuza, aho gutegereza ko hari undi umuha uburenganzira bwo kubigeraho.

Yagize ati: “Ibyo Afurika imaze kugeraho kugeza ubu byashobotse kubera ko twafashe inshingano zo kwiyubakira ejo hazaza hacu.”

Yakomeje avuga ko kugira ngo ibyo Afurika imaze kugeraho bikomeze kuramba, Abanyafurika badakwiye gutegereza ko ibibazo bahanganye na byo bizikemura cyangwa ko isi izahindura imyitwarire yo kutita ku bibazo byabo.

Ahubwo, yasabye urubyiruko kwibanda ku byo rushobora kugenzura, birimo guhitamo indangagaciro nziza ziruranga, kuzubahiriza no kuzigenderaho rudateshuka.

Perezida Kagame kandi yagaragaje ko igihe umuntu yiyemeje kwishyiriraho intego zisumbuyeho no gukora ibirenze ibyo yari asanzwe akora, aba afunguye n’inzira y’ibishoboka ku bandi bamukikije.

Yabwiye urubyiruko ko rufite imbaraga zo kuzamura urwego rw’ibishoboka muri Afurika no ku isi, bityo ko rukwiye kuzikoresha neza.

Perezida Kagame yanagarutse ku ruhare rw’urubyiruko mu kwihangira imirimo no gushaka ibisubizo by’ibibazo Afurika ihanganye na byo.

Yavuze ko hafi kimwe cya kane cy’Abanyafurika bafite imyaka yo gukora bafite imishinga y’ubucuruzi cyangwa bari mu nzira yo kuyitangiza, igipimo yavuze ko kiri hejuru ugereranyije n’icyo mu yindi migabane y’isi.

Yagaragaje ko kuba kwagura no guteza imbere iyo mishinga bikomeje kuba imbogamizi bitavuga ko Afurika ibura ibitekerezo bishya cyangwa ubushobozi bwo guhanga udushya, ahubwo ko hakwiye no kurebwa ku zindi nzitizi zirimo gukorera mu dutsiko no kudafatanya.

Yasabye urubyiruko kumva ko ubufatanye ari ingenzi, agaragaza ko zimwe muri sosiyete zikomeye zahinduye byinshi ku isi zitubatswe n’abantu bakorera ukwabo, ahubwo ko zashinzwe n’abantu basangiye icyerekezo bagakorera hamwe kuva mu ntangiriro.

Yagize ati: “Na mwe turabasaba gukora mutyo, kuko tuzi kandi twizeye ko mubishoboye.”

Yashishikarije urubyiruko gukorana umwete, gukomeza kwicisha bugufi no kudateshuka ku ntego rwihaye, agaragaza ko inshingano z’abayobozi ari ugushyigikira urubyiruko no kurufasha kugera ku byo rwiyemeje.

Yagize ati: “Kuba abantu babategerejeho gukora byinshi kurushaho si ikibazo, ahubwo ni ikimenyetso cy’uko hari byinshi mushobora kubageraho.”

President Paul Kagame has urged African countries to strengthen collaboration, invest in local talent and develop the infrastructure needed to become equal partners in the global development of artificial intelligence (AI) and other emerging technologies.

Speaking during the YouthConnekt Africa Summit 2026, Kagame said Africa has the human talent and technical expertise to participate meaningfully in developing advanced technologies rather than remaining a passive consumer of innovations produced elsewhere.

He noted that Africans are already working within some of the world’s leading technology companies, demonstrating that the continent has engineers, data analysts and innovators capable of contributing to the next generation of technological advancements.

“There is no reason why Africa should be disconnected from this when we actually have all these things. The only thing we need to do is to come together, deploy them, develop them, and make sure they work for us,” Kagame said.

The President emphasized the need for stronger partnerships between governments, the private sector and technology professionals, alongside greater investment in infrastructure, skills development and access to financing.

He also challenged African countries to reconsider their position in international technology partnerships, arguing that the continent should move beyond being a junior partner and take an equal role in shaping the technologies that increasingly influence economies and societies.

“We can’t always be the junior partners in everything. I think we have to be equal partners at one point,” he said.

Kagame called on young people, governments and businesses to take responsibility for mobilising the continent’s existing expertise and turning it into practical solutions that address Africa’s development challenges.

On artificial intelligence, he acknowledged its rapidly expanding potential to transform sectors such as medicine, agriculture and transportation, while warning that its benefits must be balanced against the risks associated with its use.

He stressed the importance of putting appropriate safeguards in place, particularly regarding safety, privacy and the responsible management of emerging technologies.

“AI is the way to go, but we need to put in place certain protections that will minimize the dangers they carry with them,” Kagame said.

He maintained that Africa has the capacity to benefit from technological advancement and shape its future, provided countries move beyond discussions and commit to meaningful cooperation, investment and implementation.

Watford have appointed former Romania boss Edward Iordanescu as the Championship club's new head coach.

The 48-year-old replaces Alessio Dionisi, who was sacked on Sunday after only five months in charge following a run of seven defeats in their past 10 league games, culminating in Saturday's 4-0 loss to Sheffield United.

"I am very proud and happy to be at this football club," Iordanescu told the club website. , external

"I can see the team is in a difficult moment but I have already watched many of the games over the last few days and I'm very confident about the future."

He becomes Watford's sixth new boss in less than 18 months and is the 25th manager since the Pozzo family took over the club in 2012.

The former CFR Cluj and Legia Warsaw manager will be joined at Watford by backroom staff Alexandru Radu, Grzegorz Mokry and Michele Iannucci, but will watch Wednesday's Championship match at home to Blackburn Rovers from the stands before taking charge for Saturday's game at Derby.

Adrian Mariappa will oversee Wednesday's match at Vicarage Road (19:45 GMT), alongside Paul Furlong and Lloyd Doyley.

Umukobwa ukiri muto wo muri Mozambique witabiriye inama ya YouthConnekt Africa Summit i Kigali, yashimiye Perezida Paul Kagame n’Ingabo z’u Rwanda (RDF) ku ruhare bagize mu kugarura umutekano mu Ntara ya Cabo Delgado, avuga ko byafashije urubyiruko kongera gushora imari muri ako gace.

Luciana, ukora ubuvugizi akaba na rwiyemezamirimo muri Mozambique, yabivugiye imbere ya Perezida Kagame ubwo yabazaga ikibazo mu kiganiro cyahuje abayobozi bakuru n’urubyiruko rwitabiriye iyi nama.

Yabanje gushimira Perezida Kagame ku byo yavuze ko u Rwanda rwakoze muri Cabo Delgado, aho RDF yoherejwe mu 2021 gufasha Mozambique guhangana n’ibitero by’abarwanyi.

Yagize ati “Mbere na mbere ndashaka gushimira Nyakubahwa Perezida Paul Kagame ku kazi keza yakoze i Cabo Delgado akoresheje Ingabo z’u Rwanda.”

Luciana yavuze ko ubufatanye bw’u Rwanda na Mozambique mu bijyanye n’umutekano bwatumye urubyiruko rutangira kongera kubona amahirwe yo gushora imari muri Cabo Delgado.

Ati “Ubu dufite urubyiruko rwinshi rushora imari muri Cabo Delgado kubera ubu bufatanye bw’Ingabo z’u Rwanda.”

U Rwanda rwohereje ingabo n’abapolisi muri Cabo Delgado muri Nyakanga 2021, ku busabe bwa Guverinoma ya Mozambique, mu rwego rwo gufasha guhangana n’inyeshyamba zari zimaze imyaka ziteza umutekano muke muri ako gace.

Kuva icyo gihe, RDF yagize uruhare mu bikorwa bihuriweho n’inzego z’umutekano za Mozambique, birimo kugarura umutekano mu bice byari byarafashwe n’inyeshyamba no kurinda abaturage n’ibikorwa by’ingenzi.

Yasabye koroshya ingendo z’abacuruzi bato

Luciana kandi yabwiye Perezida Kagame n’abandi bakuru b’ibihugu bari baje muri YouthConnekt Africa 26 ko imwe mu mbogamizi urubyiruko rw’abacuruzi ruhura na zo muri Afurika ari ibiciro by’ingendo n’inzitizi zo kwambuka imipaka.

Yavuze ko afite inshuti muri Lesotho, Ethiopia na Zimbabwe zisaba ibicuruzwa byo muri Mozambique, ariko ko hari ibibazo by’ubwikorezi n’ingendo bituma adashobora kwagura ubucuruzi bwe muri ibyo bihugu.

Yasabye ko hakorwa uburyo bworohereza ba rwiyemezamirimo bato biyandikishije kandi batanga imisoro kubona ingendo zihenze make hagati y’ibihugu bya Afurika.

Ati “Ndasaba ko mwatekereza ku buryo itike z’indege zagabanywa ku bacuruzi biyandikishije.”

Yavuze ko adasaba ko imipaka ifungurwa ku buryo budafite igenzura, ahubwo ko hakwiye kubaho uburyo bwo kumenya abagenda, cyane cyane abacuruzi bafite ibyangombwa kandi bakishyura imisoro.

Luciana yavuze ko mu gihugu cye icyangombwa gihabwa umuntu cyangwa sosiyete yemeza ko ikora ubucuruzi mu buryo bwemewe kandi ikishyura imisoro gishobora gufasha mu koroshya uru rugendo.

Yavuze ko koroshya ingendo nk’izi byafasha urubyiruko kwagura ubucuruzi no gutanga umusanzu mu kubaka Afurika yifuza.

Ku ruhande rwe, umwe mu bayobozi bari muri iki kiganiro yavuze ko Afurika ikwiye kwihutisha ivugurura rigamije koroshya urujya n’uruza rw’abantu n’ibicuruzwa, ashimangira ko urubyiruko ari umutungo ukomeye w’umugabane.

Yavuze ko ibihugu bikwiye gushyiraho uburyo butuma urubyiruko rubasha kugenda no gukora ubucuruzi mu bihugu bitandukanye, aho guhora rutegeje igihe kirekire ngo impinduka zigerweho.

Ati “Tugomba kwihuta. Tugomba kwirinda gusezeranya ibintu tuzakora mu gihe kirekire kandi dushobora kubikora uyu munsi.”

Yasabye urubyiruko na rwo gufata inshingano zo kubaka ahazaza harwo, avuga ko buri gisekuru kigomba kugira uruhare mu kugena aho Afurika igana.

Mu gusubiza iki kibazo kijyanye n’ingendo zihenze, Alexandre Barro Chambrier, yavuze ko barimo gukora ibishoboka byose ngo bashyireho uburyo bufasha urubyiruko gukorana hagati yarwo.

Yagize ati “Uyu munsi dufite ubufatanye hagati ya RwandAir na Fly Gabon bugomba kurushaho koroshya ubuhahirane, kandi turimo gukora ibishoboka byose ngo dukureho inzitizi zabuzaga abantu kugenda.”

Yavuze ko Afurika ifite abaturage benshi, biganjemo urubyiruko, kandi ko kugira abaturage benshi ari inyungu Afurika igomba kubyaza umusaruro.

KIGALI – Africa’s growing entrepreneurial activity will not automatically translate into stronger businesses and more jobs unless young entrepreneurs learn to work together, President Paul Kagame has said.

Speaking at the opening of the eighth YouthConnekt Africa Summit in Kigali on Wednesday, November 25, Kagame challenged the youth to move beyond isolated efforts and build enterprises through collaboration.

The Head of State said nearly a quarter of Africa’s working-age population is actively running or starting a business, the highest rate globally.

However, he argued that the continent’s challenge is increasingly about turning that entrepreneurial energy into businesses capable of growing and making a wider economic impact.

“If scaling remains a problem, the story these numbers tell is that ideas and creativity aren’t what’s missing. Beyond the structural barriers we all know about, we often fail to talk about how working in silos is holding you back,” Kagame told his audience.

“Remember that some of the most transformational companies on this planet were not built in isolation but through collaboration. They were built from the ground up by individuals who shared a vision. We need you to do the same because we know and trust that you can,” he added.

His remarks put collaboration alongside the more widely discussed obstacles facing African entrepreneurs, including access to finance, business regulations and the difficulty of reaching larger markets.

Kagame said the relationship between African leaders and young people must also be based on shared responsibility, with governments creating an environment in which businesses can thrive while young people take advantage of available opportunities.

“Leaders must eliminate barriers with good policies, and youth must take advantage of the opportunities created for them,” he said. Young Africans, he said, must take greater ownership of their future rather than wait for external circumstances to change.

The President urged young people to maintain high standards and remain committed to the values that guide their work, saying individual responsibility also influences what becomes possible for others.

“Real success begins when you build the life you want for yourself without waiting for anyone’s permission. Africa’s progress has depended on taking ownership of its own future,” he noted.

From Business Ideas to Continental Markets

The need to connect young entrepreneurs to financing and larger markets was also highlighted by Dr. Matthias Naab, Director of UNDP’s Regional Service Centre for Africa and Co-Chair of YouthConnekt Africa.

He said Africa’s young people need more than entrepreneurship programs, but also having their ideas connected to the resources and institutions required to turn them into sustainable businesses.

“They need ecosystems that connect their ideas and ambitions to finance, markets, leadership opportunities and lasting impact,” Naab said.

He identified investment in future-ready skills, unlocking financing and markets, and giving young people a meaningful role in shaping policies and institutions as three priorities for advancing Africa’s youth agenda.

The emphasis on market access comes as African countries seek to make the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) work for businesses beyond national borders.

Naab said UNDP and the YouthConnekt Africa Hub had, over the preceding two days, brought together hundreds of young entrepreneurs and traders to develop export action plans and propose solutions to trade barriers under the continental trade framework.

The exercise is intended to help young businesses identify opportunities beyond their domestic markets and address some of the obstacles that limit their participation in regional trade.

For entrepreneurs seeking to expand, access to customers across African countries could provide a larger market for their products and services, although this also requires the financing, skills and business capacity to compete.

A Homegrown Initiative with Continental Reach

The summit also reflects the expansion of YouthConnekt from a Rwandan initiative into a continental platform.

Nearly a decade after its establishment in Rwanda, the initiative now operates in 39 African countries, connecting young people to opportunities, institutions and decision-makers.

Naab said the initiative’s next phase should focus on translating those connections into tangible economic opportunities, rather than measuring success by the number of programs and discussions held.

He pointed to Rwanda’s Aguka Program, which supports youth-led businesses and job creation, as one example of efforts to advance this agenda.

He also highlighted UNDP’s Pan-African Timbuktoo initiative, including its Timbuktoo HealthTech Hub in Kigali and University Innovation Pods (UniPods), which support young innovators in developing and scaling their ideas into businesses.

The summit, held under the theme “Shaping the Generational Mission”, brings together young leaders, policymakers, investors and development partners from across the continent. The three-day summit runs from November 25 to 27, 2026.

The summit has brought together young people from various African countries at the Kigali Convention Centre, alongside policymakers, business leaders, development partners and civil society representatives.

Discussions over the three days will focus on cross-border trade, technology, e-commerce, skills development and strategies for expanding employment opportunities, with young people expected to play an active role in shaping solutions to the challenges they face.

YouthConnekt was launched by the Government of Rwanda in 2017 in partnership with the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP).

AJ Odudu said being called aggressive was "very harsh" and it was "an insane word" to use about her

More than 800 people have complained to the media regulator about an episode of ITV reality show I'm A Celebrity... Get Me Out of Here! in which Mariella Frostrup accused her campmate AJ Odudu of being "aggressive".

Tensions first flared between the pair as they were seen cooking together on Saturday, before both were reduced to tears when the friction escalated the following morning.

Ofcom said 887 people had filed complaints about Sunday's episode in relation to "alleged bullying behaviour" by Frostrup towards Odudu.

The pair were seen clearing the air on Tuesday, with broadcaster Frostrup saying she was "sorry for calling you aggressive" and Odudu telling her it is "a strong word to use in casual scenarios, particularly towards black women".

Wayne Rooney tried to repair relations between AJ Odudu (left) and Mariella Frostrup on Sunday

An Ofcom spokesperson told BBC News: "We are assessing the complaints against our rules, but are yet to decide whether or not to investigate."

In Sunday's instalment of the programme, Odudu said she felt being called aggressive was "very harsh" and it was "an insane word" to use about her, and that "it is just such a triggering word".

In an amicable conversation in Tuesday's episode, she told Frostrup: "It's triggering because in this world, navigating it as a person who looks like me can be difficult sometimes because my experience is that my emotions and my intent are completely misconstrued.

"In same way that you are allowed to express yourself, I can't express myself in the same way. We're not granted the same freedom.

"You're allowed to be emotional and passionate, and I automatically go to 'aggressive'. There's no in-between. It's like I'm 'dramatic' and 'aggressive' and that's it.

"Whereas I feel like someone like you gets to go through all the emotions of life and all of those emotions are accepted and embraced and valid."

Mariella Frostrup risked further tension when she told Odudu that "you don't take an apology well"

Frostrup replied that she thought being labelled "agressive" was "a woman thing more than anything else".

"I think women who speak their mind and are forthright, that's 'aggressive', whereas a man who speaks his mind and is forthright is a 'strong man'," she said, but added that "I totally get that there's more" when race is involved.

Odudu responded: "I do definitely see your point and agree with it, but those words stick as well. Those words can stick for us. The moment passes for you and it doesn't pass for me."

Odudu replied: "Well, I wasn't being aggressive, so it shouldn't have been there."

Signs of friction resurfaced when Frostrup told Odudu that "you don't take an apology well".

Odudu replied that "of course" she had accepted her apology, before Frostrup accepted that "it's really important to me to understand why it's triggering".

Odudu added: "It's good you asked, but it's a strong word to use in casual scenarios, particularly towards black women."

Many viewers defended Odudu after the pair's earlier encounter.

They included former BBC Radio 1 DJ Clara Amfo, who said: "Calling a black woman 'aggressive' when she is being anything else but is a classic microaggression."

Singer Beverley Knight wrote: "The word 'aggressive' feeds directly into the 'angry Black woman' trope. It IS hurtful and offensive."

Speaking on spin-off show I'm A Celebrity... Unpacked on Sunday, former campmate Jordan Banjo said Frostrup had handled the situation "poorly", but urged people to "give a bit of grace to Mariella, and everyone in the camp" because "you can't judge an abnormal situation by normal standards".

It is "a really weird situation that every single person's in, and I'm not sure if people go at stuff with the clearest head", he said, explaining: "You get these weird breakdowns, and I think that's literally what we're seeing."

An ITV statement said: "The production monitors everyone in camp 24/7 and if at any time we feel someone has overstepped the line by using inappropriate language or displaying unacceptable behaviour, we would take steps to intervene and speak to everyone involved.

"The duty of care for our contestants is of the utmost importance to us. We take the welfare of the celebrities very seriously and have measures in place to ensure they are supported at every stage of the process: before, during and after filming."

Watch: Moment Raheem Sterling arrested after car crash

Former England footballer Raheem Sterling has been handed a suspended sentence after he crashed his Lamborghini.

The 31-year-old, from Berkshire, gave no reaction as he was sentenced to 12 months imprisonment, suspended for 18 months, at Basingstoke Magistrates' Court for dangerous driving and possessing nitrous oxide on 28 May.

Sterling pleaded guilty in September to driving a Lamborghini Urus dangerously on the M25, the M3, the A327 and Minley Road.

He also admitted possession of six nitrous oxide canisters for wrongful inhalation, a Class C drug, and failing to provide a specimen.

Sterling was ordered to complete 100 hours unpaid work and was banned from driving for 24 months.

He was arrested after crashing near the M3 in Hampshire.

During the previous hearing, prosecutor Simon Jones said a number of calls were made between 07:45 and 08:52 BST about a black sports car and the manner it was being driven.

Footage was released of the footballer driving dangerously

Witness Christopher Jennings called 999 after driving alongside Sterling's car on the M25, and "he was shocked by what he saw", Jones said, and made clear "he sighted the defendant inhaling from the balloon".

Fiona Jennings – driving on the southbound M3 – described the driving as "absolutely horrendous" and "swerving in and out of lanes", the court heard.

Sterling most recently played for Feyenoord in the Dutch Eredivisie, having left Chelsea in January, but made just eight appearances in the Netherlands.

In four years at Chelsea - including a season-long loan at Arsenal - he made 59 league appearances after signing from Manchester City in 2022.

With City he won four Premier League titles, having started his senior career with Liverpool before moving to Manchester in 2015.

In the 2021 Queen's Birthday Honours, Sterling was made an MBE for services to racial equality in sport.

Muri Repubulika iharanira Demokarasi ya Congo, intambara ikomeje kwaguka igera mu bice bitandukanye, kuko ubu Umutwe wa FRN/M23 winjiye muri Teritwari ya Lubero muri Kivu y’Amajyaruguru, mu buryo butunguranye, kuko ingabo za Leta FARDC zitari zibyiteze na gato.

Ubusanzwe, iyo teritwari ya Lubero nk’uko bisobanurwa na Nibishaka Jean Baptiste, umunyamakuru wa Kigali Today uri muri Repubulika ya Demokarasi ya Congo, ni yo teritwari iri ku mpera muri Kivu y’Amajyaruguru, ikaba ihana imbibe na Taritwari ya Walikale. Muri iyo Teritwari ya Lubero kandi, igice kimwe cyamaze kubohorwa kiri ku ruhande rugenzurwa na FRN, mu gihe ikindi gice kiri ku ruhande rugenzurwa na Leta.

Aho muri Teritwari ya Lubero, FRN/M23, yafashe agace kitwa Kanjanja, ubwo bukaba ari nk’uburyo bwo bwihuse bwo gushaka uko yakwinjira muri Walikale,gukomeza ugana za Kisangani.

Nubwo ingabo za FARDC ziri kumwe n’ingabo z’Abarundi n’abandi bafatanyije muri Kivu y’Amajyepfo, ariko ngo ntabwo byakorohera izo ngabo guhita zigera muri Kivu y’Amajyaruguru muri Lubero. Aho rero, igishoboka ngo ni uko FARDC yarwana ifatanyije na FDLR n’abacanshuro b’abanyamahanga.

Ntabwo FARDC yatekerezaga ko FRN yatera muri ako gace ka Lubero, kuba FRN yahateye bitunguranye, ngo nibyo byatumye ihita ifata ahitwa Kanjanja, ndetse n’imirwano ikaba yakomereje ahitwa Runzenze ku mugoroba wo kuri uyu wa 24 Ugushyingo 2026, mu gihe yatangiye saa kumi zo mu rukerera.

Kanjanja na Runzenze twombi ni uduce tubarizwa muri Teritwari ya Lubero, ako gace karimo kuberamo imirwano, ngo ntabwo ari kure y’Ikiyaga cya Edouard kizwiho cyane kuba gikorerwamo uburobyi bukomeye, kuko ngo ni mu bilometero 40 kugira ngo ukigereho.

Kuba umutwe wa FRN/M23 watangiye kugira utundi duce ufata muri Teritwari ya Lubero, ngo byateye impungenge cyane, kubera ko bishobora gutuma iyo mirwano igera ahitwa Kyavinyonge. Kandi FRN iramutse yageze aho i Kyavinyonge ngo yaba ishobora no kugera mu yindi Mijyi ikomeye nka Kasindi na Beni yombi iherereye muri Teritwari ya Beni, muri Kivu y’Amajyaruguru.

The 27 mayors elected to lead Rwanda’s districts outside Kigali face a broad set of responsibilities, from managing local services and development projects to responding to residents’ concerns and accounting for public spending.

A district mayor leads the district’s Executive Committee and coordinates the work of different institutions.

The role includes overseeing development, implementing government policies and ensuring that residents receive services effectively. But mayors must often deliver results while working with limited budgets and staffing constraints.

Their daily duties include monitoring district employees and sector executive secretaries, reviewing reports from local authorities and directing action on issues that require district support.

They are also expected to address disputes among staff or institutions, deal with poor performance and ensure that services are delivered on time.

The role requires balancing competing interests and coordinating people with different responsibilities. When a service is delayed or a local problem remains unresolved, residents often turn to the mayor, even when another institution is responsible for handling it.

Limited resources can make development targets difficult to meet.

Districts may need to build roads and other infrastructure, improve access to clean water and electricity, and address housing challenges, while lacking the funds to carry out every planned project.

Mayors must also oversee district budgets, prevent waste or misuse of public funds and track whether projects are completed on schedule.

When a project falls behind, the cause may include insufficient funding, staff or technical capacity, unavailable equipment, or a contractor’s failure to meet agreed terms.

Mayors are expected to identify the problem and work with relevant institutions to find a solution. Attracting investors and development partners can also help districts expand their capacity.

Residents bring mayors a wide range of concerns, including poor services, land and property disputes, family and community conflicts, poverty, unemployment and inadequate housing.

Some requests may fall beyond a district’s authority or resources, requiring mayors to explain where responsibility lies and connect residents with the appropriate institutions.

Mayors are also accountable for district performance and public finances.

They must report to higher authorities and oversight bodies, work towards district performance targets, follow government regulations and act on recommendations from the Office of the Auditor General.

An analysis released by Transparency International Rwanda in April 2026 identified weaknesses in public procurement, asset management and compliance with laws in local government institutions.

Meeting performance targets can be difficult when funding is inadequate, projects are delayed, contractors fail to deliver, or districts lack equipment and technical expertise.

Extreme weather can also damage development infrastructure. At the same time, districts are expected to address social needs, including child malnutrition and stunting, sanitation, support for vulnerable households, and coordination with health and education institutions.

A Ministry of Local Government report reviewing 25 years of decentralised governance, from 2000 to 2025, identified challenges including staff shortages, skills gaps in some institutions, high employee turnover, limited digital skills and weaknesses in project monitoring and evaluation.

Mayors cannot achieve district targets alone. They must work with ministries and other government agencies, security services, health and education institutions, businesses, investors, civil society organisations and local leaders from sector to village level.

When these partners disagree on priorities or fail to carry out agreed actions, district programmes can stall.

Although the mayor leads the district’s Executive Committee, responsibility for local government is shared with the District Council, the district executive secretary and other officials.

Yet, as the district’s most visible senior executive, the mayor is often the person residents and authorities look to when things go wrong.

The Minister of Interior, Dr Vincent Biruta, has urged the Rwanda National Police to maintain the professionalism and standards expected of the force as its senior leaders review the institution’s performance and priorities.

Biruta made the call while opening the National Police Council meeting at the Police headquarters in Kacyiru, Kigali. The council is the force’s highest decision-making body, bringing together senior police leaders, heads of departments and units, and officials from across the country.

The meeting provides an opportunity to assess the force’s work, identify areas that need improvement and agree on measures to address them.

The council also sets policy direction, monitors police performance, approves long-term plans and annual programmes, and reviews reports on the force’s activities.

The meeting comes as the Rwanda National Police pursues efforts to strengthen professional conduct, ethical leadership and accountability.

On November 23, the force, in partnership with the Commonwealth Secretariat, began a week-long training programme for 36 senior officers.

The training focuses on leadership, planning, integrity, professional conduct and accountability, including ways to address corruption in law enforcement.

Regional cooperation is also a priority. On November 17, the Rwanda National Police and the Uganda Police Force signed a three-year agreement to strengthen crime prevention, intelligence sharing, border security and joint operations.

The agreement covers cooperation against terrorism, human trafficking, drug trafficking, cybercrime, economic crimes and criminal networks operating across national borders.

Other broad security priorities include preventing crime, improving road safety, using technology to investigate and combat offences, building public trust and strengthening police capacity to respond to new and cross-border threats.

These are wider challenges facing the security sector and should not be taken as a confirmed list of items on the council’s agenda.

The National Police Council serves as a forum for senior leaders to review how the force can better protect people and their property, prevent crime and contribute to peace and stability.

Raheem Sterling has scored 123 goals in 396 Premier League appearances and provided 65 assists

Raheem Sterling grew up a stone's throw from Wembley Stadium, and went on to start a European Championship final for England there.

At his peak, the four-time Premier League winner was earning £325,000 a week at Chelsea .

"Raheem is a huge player with a huge influence in the last few years in English football," said then Blues boss Thomas Tuchel when he signed a 27-year-old Sterling in a £50m deal in 2022.

"He is at the perfect age to take responsibility around the younger players that we have and be an example.

"He just needs to do what he did over the last few years and he will be a huge asset for us."

Sterling enjoyed a 10-year England career, also played for Liverpool , Manchester City and Arsenal , and commanded combined transfer fees of about £100m.

But his career at the top level of English football looks to be in the balance at the age of 31 after he was handed a 12-month prison sentence, suspended for 18 months, for dangerous driving. Sterling has also been disqualified from driving for two years and ordered to carry out 100 hours of unpaid work.

At an earlier hearing in September, Sterling admitted dangerous driving on a motorway before crashing a Lamborghini on 28 May.

The crash caused "substantial" damage to his car and all four wheels, which prevented him from driving further, the court heard.

Sterling also admitted possessing nitrous oxide for wrongful inhalation, and failing to provide a specimen for analysis.

How Sterling went from England star to court appearance

Sterling's life was touched by tragedy at a young age.

Born in Kingston, Jamaica, he was just two when his father was shot dead.

His mother, Nadine, was determined to give her children a safer environment to live in. She moved to England to lay a path for Sterling and his sister to join her once she had found a home and finished her education, while cleaning bathrooms and changing bedsheets in hotels to earn extra money.

Sterling grew up on a housing estate in Neasden, north-west London, and spent part of his education at Vernon House, where teachers attempted to help the football-obsessed youngster with behavioural problems.

In an interview with the Players' Tribune , external in 2018, Sterling said: "I was so naughty that they kicked me out of primary school. I just didn't like to listen to anyone but my mum. That was my problem."

He was 10 when teacher Chris Beschi told him: "If you carry on the way you're going, by the time you're 17 you'll either be playing for England or in prison."

Sterling would grow to become one of the standout English attacking talents of his generation.

Raheem Sterling: From school struggles to a class of his own

On 14 November 2012 - aged 17 years and 342 days - Sterling made his England debut on the night his Liverpool captain Steven Gerrard won his 100th cap in a 4-2 defeat by Sweden in Stockholm.

Sterling would go on to make 81 more appearances for his country, scoring 20 goals.

He featured at three World Cups - 2014, 2018 and 2022 - and two European Championships. He was one of the standout players as England reached the Euro 2020 final at Wembley, where they were beaten by Italy.

Sterling was now at the peak of his career - the former Queens Park Rangers youngster, who has a tattoo on his forearm of a young boy holding a football looking up at the Wembley arch, named in the team of the tournament by Uefa.

Liverpool had signed a 15-year-old Sterling from QPR for £600,000 in February 2010.

He made his senior Reds debut two years later and became the second-youngest goalscorer in their history - behind Michael Owen - when he scored the winner against Reading in October 2012 at the age of 17.

In 2015, Sterling joined Manchester City in a deal worth up to £49m, making him the most expensive English player at the time.

He had been under contract at Anfield until 2017 but turned down a new deal to move to Liverpool 's rivals, with City boss Manuel Pellegrini describing the 20-year-old as "one of the best attacking players in world football".

Sterling went on to score 131 goals in 339 appearances in all competitions during seven successful years at Etihad Stadium.

As well as four Premier League titles, he helped City win five League Cups, one FA Cup and one Community Shield.

It was while he was at City, in 2021, that Sterling became an MBE in the Queen's Birthday Honours for his services to racial equality in sport.

"I am grateful to have been recognised," he said. "But my priority is to try to help to educate society and myself. I'm learning every day."

After City came the move to Chelsea , where his career began to stall.

Tuchel, now England manager, was sacked two months after signing Sterling, who made just 45 Premier League starts for the Blues over four years.

Off the pitch, he launched a scholarship fund aimed at closing the gap in the number of black British students who go to university.

On the pitch, he was finding it a struggle.

He spent 18 months as a member of Chelsea 's so-called 'bomb squad' , and a season-long loan to Arsenal in 2024-25 proved largely unsuccessful.

Sterling: If you grew up in a certain area you feel like there's limits

As well as his success on the field, Sterling has made headlines off it too.

In 2015, when he was 20, reports began to surface about his behaviour away from the game.

Sterling was pictured apparently inhaling nitrous oxide and was also photographed smoking a shisha pipe.

That prompted then Liverpool boss Brendan Rodgers to warn Sterling he would "look back in 20 years and wonder what he was doing".

Sterling also made headlines while on duty for England at the 2018 World Cup in Russia.

The Sun ran a story titled "Raheem shoots himself in the foot" as pictures emerged of a tattoo of an M16 assault rifle on his leg.

Sterling explained on social media: "When I was 2 my father died from being gunned down to death I made a promise to myself I would never touch a gun in my life time. I shoot with my right foot so it has a deeper meaning."

The incident led to a widespread discussion in the UK about the treatment of black athletes in the media, with comparisons drawn between how Sterling's life was covered compared to others.

Sterling spoke out a number of times on the issue and wider racism in society, which was reflected in him being made an MBE.

Five years later, Sterling's career has stalled. He has not played since appearing for Feyenoord on 17 May, after agreeing a short-term move to the Netherlands.

Eleven days after that game, he was arrested after crashing a Lamborghini near the M3 in Hampshire.

Sterling was riding the crest of a wave when he moved from Manchester City to Chelsea in the summer of 2022 for £50m.

His medal cabinet was already fit to burst with 10 major trophies under Guardiola and, alongside Harry Kane, he was arguably England's most important player for then head coach Gareth Southgate.

Tuchel viewed Sterling as his number one target that summer and Chelsea 's new ownership - Behdad Eghbali and Todd Boehly - delivered as the club entered the post-Roman Abramovich era.

Two months later, Tuchel was sacked and Graham Potter was in situ.

Sterling's career has not been the same since.

It is, of course, senseless to suggest the troubles Sterling has had on and off the pitch in recent years are simply down to the sacking of Tuchel in 2022.

But speak to those close to Sterling and they will explain Tuchel was among the key factors behind the winger's decision to swap Manchester for west London.

He was captivated by Tuchel's vision, not only for the team, but his role in it.

KIGALI – Trinity Metals has started a major drilling campaign at its Rutongo mine in northern Rwanda, using specialised technology to investigate tin deposits deep underground and establish whether the mine can has more to last decades more.

The campaign, which began on November 13 at the Karambo mine, marks the first modern diamond-drilling programme in the history of Rutongo, one of Africa’s major cassiterite deposits.

The company is targeting areas below the mine’s current operating levels, hoping to identify additional mineral resources and determine how far the tin deposits extend underground.

The first phase will involve drilling between 1,800 and 2,000 metres across five holes, with the deepest expected to reach between 650 and 700 metres.

The initial programme is scheduled to take approximately three months.

The first hole had reached a depth of 75 metres at the time of the announcement.

Despite its name, diamond drilling is not used to search for diamonds. It involves a specialised diamond-tipped drill bit that cuts through rock and extracts cylindrical samples, known as cores.

Geologists examine these samples to determine the presence, quality and extent of mineral deposits.

Trinity Metals says the results will guide the development of access to deeper sections of Rutongo and help the company plan future production more accurately.

Peter Geleta, Chief Executive Officer of Trinity Metals, said in a statement on Wednesday that the campaign would provide geological information needed to unlock the mine’s deeper potential.

For almost a century, the Rutongo area has been mined without systematic modern drilling, with previous exploration largely relying on artisanal pitting and tunnelling, according to the company.

The initial drilling forms part of a larger surface exploration programme covering approximately 12,000 metres. Trinity also plans underground drilling to improve its understanding of the deposits and establish more reliable estimates of available resources.

Rutongo is located about 26 kilometres north of Kigali and comprises six underground tin mines. Its mining concession covers approximately 9,600 hectares.

The mine currently produces between 40 and 70 tonnes of tin per month. Trinity estimates that the concession contains approximately 54,000 tonnes of recoverable tin, with plans to increase monthly production to 200 tonnes over the next five years.

The new drilling programme is part of a wider exploration drive covering the company’s other operations. Trinity says drilling plans and budgets have already been prepared for Nyamyumba, Gasambya and Sanzari, while additional targets remain under consideration.

Trinity Metals was formed in 2022 through the merger of three mining businesses: Rutongo Tin Mine, Nyakabingo Tungsten Mine and Musha Tin and Tantalum Mine.

The company produces Rwanda’s three major technology minerals commonly known as the 3Ts: tin, tungsten and tantalum. It has also identified a lithium deposit, known as Ntunga, on its Musha concession.

Its exploration activities extend beyond tin. At Nyakabingo, one of Africa’s largest tungsten-producing mines, Trinity began an advanced drilling programme in May 2026 to investigate whether tungsten-bearing veins extend further underground.

That campaign targets depths of approximately 850 metres and is intended to improve estimates of the mine’s resources and support long-term production planning.

In July 2026, the company also launched a sonic-drilling programme to assess historically mined material at Nyakabingo, with the aim of identifying additional tungsten that could potentially be recovered from old stockpiles.

Trinity has also been investing in processing technology.

At Nyakabingo, it commissioned a five-tonne-per-hour pilot plant to test improved methods of recovering tungsten from ore, including finer mineral particles that can be lost through traditional processing methods.

The company employs more than 6,000 people across its Rwandan operations, according to its published figures.

Trinity’s majority shareholder is TechMet, a UK-based investment company focused on securing supplies of minerals used in modern technology and industry. TechMet works with several investment partners, including the US International Development Finance Corporation (DFC).

Trinity received US$3.865 million in technical assistance funding from the DFC in June 2024, according to the company.

Through its investments in exploration, processing and mine modernisation, Trinity is seeking to expand production and increase the amount of minerals that can be recovered from its Rwandan operations.

The unnamed surgeon took over the knee surgery from a colleague at Dr Gray's in Elgin

An NHS Grampian surgeon took over a knee operation while he was recovering from a medical procedure and under the influence of drugs, the BBC has learned.

The doctor, who had to be driven to Dr Gray's hospital in Elgin, allegedly stepped in because a colleague felt unable to complete the surgery.

In a separate incident in the same department, it is alleged that a surgeon had a physical altercation with a registrar who suggested they were about to replace the wrong hip of a patient who was lying unconscious on the operating table.

NHS Grampian said both matters were addressed at the time through the appropriate governance and employment processes, and immediate action had been taken.

The allegations, first reported in The Times , external newspaper, have emerged less than two weeks after the watchdog Healthcare Improvement Scotland (HIS) published a damning report identifying serious shortcomings with NHS Grampian's leadership.

'Dramatic action' needed after NHS Grampian leaders criticised in damning report - Swinney

The BBC has verified the first allegation involving the surgeon who was recovering from an endoscopy - a procedure where a tube with a camera attached is inserted into the body. Patients are often given a sedative for this.

He took over the knee operation after being driven from his home to the hospital, because he felt he could not drive himself.

A senior member of NHS Grampian's management team learned what was happening and removed him from the operating theatre.

The BBC has asked NHS Grampian whether the patient had been informed of the incident.

The allegations, including the claim about a separate physical altercation, were brought to the attention of former MSP Douglas Ross by a whistleblower last year.

Ross then raised both incidents with NHS Grampian chief executive, Laura Skaife-Knight, at the end of October by email.

The following week, Skaife-Knight replied that the health board "cannot respond to the specific issues" due to duty of care to individual employees.

Ross told her the response was "unacceptable" and repeatedly asked whether NHS Grampian had been "100% open, honest and transparent" with the press and public - which Skaife-Knight declines to answer.

NHS Grampian's chief officer of acute services, Geraldine Fraser, said the health board takes concerns about patient and staff safety "extremely seriously".

She said: "The matters referred to were addressed at the time through the appropriate governance and employment processes, with immediate and appropriate action taken.

"The organisation sought external support as part of its response and there has been continuing oversight of the service since, including to address workforce challenges relating to this service.

"It would be inappropriate to comment further on any employment matters about individual staff."

Speaking to the BBC, Ross said it was one of the most serious cases he had received about care in the NHS - and said Skaife-Knight had "stonewalled" him.

He said: "I was surprised, it looked like they were just building up a defensive wall. They didn't want to get to the root of the problem, they just didn't want this problem being exposed.

"I think it's come out now because when we saw the recent report into NHS Grampian and then consultants coming forward saying 'look we've been trying to warn you about this', I felt in a similar position.

"It seemed like politicians trying to represent their constituents were being treated in the exact same way as consultants trying to raise concerns – and that's not acceptable."

The HIS report about NHS Grampian, published on 12 November, found that failures to learn from mistakes had caused "repeated and avoidable harm" to patients.

A whistleblower - Dr Mohammed Habib - then leaked a 2022 review which found 19 avoidable deaths among 45 patients in liver and pancreatic surgery at Aberdeen Royal Infirmary.

The Scottish government has deployed an oversight team to help NHS Grampian make improvements, and ordered an independent review into hepatobiliary surgery at the health board.

Health Secretary Angela Constance, who was appointed to the role this year, has denied a cover-up , telling parliament this week that staff "should not carry the blame for leadership failures".

Dr Habib said he reported his concerns to the government, including letters to First Minister John Swinney.

BBC Scotland News was told that Swinney's office did not make him personally aware of the letters, with the first minister ordering a review into how his correspondence is handled.

President Paul Kagame has urged young African entrepreneurs to embrace collaboration and strengthen partnerships to overcome challenges facing businesses, particularly in expanding their enterprises and accessing wider markets.

Speaking at the YouthConnekt Africa Summit 2026, Kagame noted that although nearly a quarter of Africa’s working-age population is engaged in business and entrepreneurship, significant challenges remain in growing businesses and turning entrepreneurial initiatives into successful enterprises.

He emphasised that building successful companies requires collective effort, shared ambition and cooperation rather than individual efforts.

“Remember that the big companies in the world were not built in isolation. They were built through collaboration, by people who shared a vision. We need to do the same,” Kagame said.

He encouraged young entrepreneurs to remain committed to their ambitions, work hard and invest their energy in building businesses capable of competing beyond their local markets.

“Work hard, put in the effort, and the world will be waiting for you. Our responsibility as leaders is to support you,” he added.

Kagame’s remarks highlighted the importance of creating an enabling environment in which young entrepreneurs can access opportunities, establish meaningful partnerships and scale their businesses.

His message comes as African countries seek to harness the continent’s youthful population as a driver of economic transformation, innovation and job creation.

The United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) has called for stronger support systems that connect young Africans’ ideas and ambitions to financing, markets and leadership opportunities, stressing that programmes alone are not enough to unlock the continent’s youth potential.

Dr. Matthias Naab, UNDP Director of the Regional Service Centre for Africa, made the call while addressing the YouthConnekt Africa Summit 2026 (YCA2026), where leaders, development partners and young innovators are meeting to discuss ways of advancing youth empowerment and economic opportunities across the continent.

Naab emphasised the need to move beyond isolated youth initiatives towards comprehensive ecosystems that enable young people to turn their ideas into viable enterprises, access markets and contribute meaningfully to development.

“Africa’s young people do not simply need programs, they need ecosystems that connect their ideas and ambitions to finance, markets, leadership opportunities and lasting impact,” he said.

His remarks highlight the importance of coordinated efforts by governments, development institutions and the private sector to create an enabling environment in which young Africans can access the resources, networks and opportunities needed to realise their potential.

With Africa home to one of the world’s youngest populations, strengthening youth entrepreneurship, access to finance and participation in decision-making remains central to unlocking the continent’s demographic dividend.

President Paul Kagame has urged African countries to strengthen collaboration, invest in local talent and develop the infrastructure needed to become equal partners in the global development of artificial intelligence (AI) and other emerging technologies.

Speaking during the YouthConnekt Africa Summit 2026, Kagame said Africa has the human talent and technical expertise to participate meaningfully in developing advanced technologies rather than remaining a passive consumer of innovations produced elsewhere.

He noted that Africans are already working within some of the world’s leading technology companies, demonstrating that the continent has engineers, data analysts and innovators capable of contributing to the next generation of technological advancements.

“There is no reason why Africa should be disconnected from this when we actually have all these things. The only thing we need to do is to come together, deploy them, develop them, and make sure they work for us,” Kagame said.

The President emphasized the need for stronger partnerships between governments, the private sector and technology professionals, alongside greater investment in infrastructure, skills development and access to financing.

He also challenged African countries to reconsider their position in international technology partnerships, arguing that the continent should move beyond being a junior partner and take an equal role in shaping the technologies that increasingly influence economies and societies.

“We can’t always be the junior partners in everything. I think we have to be equal partners at one point,” he said.

Kagame called on young people, governments and businesses to take responsibility for mobilising the continent’s existing expertise and turning it into practical solutions that address Africa’s development challenges.

On artificial intelligence, he acknowledged its rapidly expanding potential to transform sectors such as medicine, agriculture and transportation, while warning that its benefits must be balanced against the risks associated with its use.

He stressed the importance of putting appropriate safeguards in place, particularly regarding safety, privacy and the responsible management of emerging technologies.

“AI is the way to go, but we need to put in place certain protections that will minimize the dangers they carry with them,” Kagame said.

He maintained that Africa has the capacity to benefit from technological advancement and shape its future, provided countries move beyond discussions and commit to meaningful cooperation, investment and implementation.
